title: Everyone affected means server config, not one account's files
explanation: If this were a StrictModes permissions issue or a wrong `AuthorizedKeysFile` path, it would hit one user's account, not every key login on the box at once. A blanket failure across all users points at a single server-wide setting rather than anything per-user.

title: Ask sshd for its effective, merged setting
explanation: `sudo sshd -T | grep -i pubkey` dumps what sshd actually believes after merging the main config with every drop-in — here, `pubkeyauthentication no`. This is faster and more reliable than reading `sshd_config` files individually, since a later drop-in can silently override an earlier setting.

title: Trace the setting to its actual source
explanation: `sudo grep -rin pubkeyauthentication /etc/ssh/sshd_config /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/` finds it in `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/hardening.conf` — a 'security hardening' change that disabled the very authentication method it should have been strengthening, entirely disabling public-key auth in favor of whatever password fallback exists.

title: Flip the directive back and validate before it takes effect
explanation: Editing the line to `PubkeyAuthentication yes` and running `sudo sshd -t` first catches any typo before it can take down SSH entirely — unlike `AuthorizedKeysFile`, this is a config-level directive that requires a reload, not something read fresh per connection.

title: Reload and confirm with the original failing command
explanation: `sudo service ssh reload` (or `sudo kill -HUP $(cat /run/sshd.pid)`) applies the change, and retrying `ssh -i ~/deploy_key deploy@localhost` confirms key login actually succeeds again rather than trusting the config value alone.
